# The Honest Lie of Maps

Every map is a lie, and the best ones are honest about it.

I don't mean that maps are wrong, though many have been. I mean that a map is only useful because it refuses to tell the whole truth. A map that included everything (every blade of grass, every parked car, every stray dog crossing the road at 4:15 on a Tuesday) would be no better than the territory it described. Its value lies in what it throws away. Making a map is an act of editing, and editing is an act of opinion.

I've been thinking about this because maps sit at an odd crossroads of human activity. They are science and art, but also argument, propaganda, memory, and hope. Looking at how people have drawn the world tells you a great deal about what they thought was worth noticing.

## The Problem of the Orange Peel

Start with the basic difficulty. The Earth is a sphere, more or less, and paper is flat. You cannot flatten a sphere without distorting it. This is not a limit of technology but a theorem, the kind of fact that holds no matter how clever you are. Try to press an orange peel flat on a table and it tears or stretches. Every map projection is a decision about where to put the tearing and stretching.

The most famous decision was made in 1569 by Gerardus Mercator, a Flemish cartographer who wanted to help sailors. His projection has a marvelous property: a line of constant compass bearing appears as a straight line on the map. If you want to sail from Lisbon to Recife, you draw a line, measure its angle, hold that heading, and arrive. For navigation in the age of sail, this was a gift.

The price was area. As you move away from the equator, Mercator's map inflates everything. Greenland appears about the size of Africa, when Africa is actually fourteen times larger. Europe looks grand, and the tropics look modest. Alaska seems to rival the contiguous United States in scale.

Mercator did not intend to insult the equatorial world. He solved a specific problem for specific users. But maps outlive their purposes. The Mercator projection went on to hang in classrooms for centuries, teaching generations of children a subtly false picture of the relative size of continents. A tool built for sailors became a worldview by accident.

Later critics proposed alternatives. The Gall–Peters projection preserves area but stretches shapes into something like dripping taffy, with Africa long and Europe squat. Arno Peters promoted it in the 1970s as a corrective to Eurocentrism, and the argument became heated, since cartographers pointed out that his map was not new and had its own distortions. Both sides had a point. Anyone claiming that a map is neutral is fooling themselves, and anyone claiming that one distortion is morally superior to another has usually forgotten to ask what the map is for.

## Jerusalem in the Middle

Consider a very different sort of map, the Hereford Mappa Mundi, made around 1300 and still displayed in Hereford Cathedral in England. It is drawn on a single sheet of calfskin and is enormous, about five feet by four. If you tried to use it to travel anywhere, you would be lost by lunchtime. Europe is squeezed into one corner. Britain is a small blob at the edge. East is at the top, which is the origin of the word "orient," meaning to face east. Jerusalem sits at the center, because that is where the map's makers believed the world's meaning was centered.

It is easy to smile at the Mappa Mundi. But that would be a mistake, because it is not a bad version of a modern road atlas. It is a different kind of thing altogether. It shows Eden at the top, monstrous races at the fringes, the Tower of Babel, the Golden Fleece, the labyrinth of Crete, and famous cities alongside biblical episodes. It is a map of time as much as of space, a diagram of everything a devout medieval person wanted to hold in mind at once. Its question was not "How do I get from here to there?" but "Where do I stand in the story of everything?"

There is a modern prejudice that maps ought to be about navigation, and that maps of anything else are somehow deficient. But the impulse behind the Mappa Mundi is very much alive. When we draw a family tree, a flowchart of an organization, a "map" of the political spectrum, or a diagram of the internet, we're doing the same thing: arranging knowledge spatially so that the mind can hold it.

And "Here be dragons," incidentally, is nearly a myth. The phrase, in Latin *HC SVNT DRACONES*, appears on the Hunt-Lenox Globe from around 1510, and as far as anyone knows it's essentially the only well-attested example on an old map. Mapmakers did sometimes decorate empty spaces with sea serpents and beasts, but the popular idea of a medieval cartographer scrawling warnings at the edge of the known world is mostly a modern invention. We like to imagine that our ancestors filled their ignorance with monsters. The reality is subtler: they often filled it with decoration, or with honesty, leaving blank spaces where they didn't know.

## The Map That Deleted the Map

Now jump to 1931, when a draftsman named Harry Beck, working for the London Underground, made a drawing in his spare time. At that point the Tube map was a geographic map with train lines laid over the streets, and as the system expanded into the suburbs, it had become a tangle. The central stations were crammed together while the outer ones sprawled.

Beck's insight was that a person in a tunnel does not care about geography. They care about sequence: which station comes next, and where they can change lines. So he did something radical. He straightened the lines to run only vertically, horizontally, or at forty-five degrees. He evened out the spacing between stations. He enlarged the crowded center and shrank the outskirts. The river Thames became a tidy ribbon. The result looked more like an electrical circuit diagram than a map, which fits, since Beck worked as an engineering draftsman.

The Underground's publicity department was initially unsure, and it rejected the design at first. When a trial version was printed in 1933, the public loved it. Nearly every subway map in the world now descends from it.

It also lies, gloriously. Stations that appear a short hop apart may be a long walk from each other. Leicester Square and Covent Garden are famously only a few hundred meters apart, and people ride the train between them, having been misled by a map that suggested a longer journey. Beck's diagram makes a perfect trade: it gives up distance to gain clarity about connection. It is the map of a relationship, not a place.

I find this one of the most instructive stories in design. The best map isn't the one that contains the most truth. It's the one that has decided which truth its user needs.

## Dots on a Street

If a map can mislead, it can also reveal, and my favorite demonstration comes from Soho, London, in the late summer of 1854. Cholera was killing people in staggering numbers. The prevailing theory held that the disease spread through "miasma," bad air rising from filth and decay. A physician named John Snow doubted this. He suspected contaminated water.

Snow interviewed residents, collected records of the dead, and marked each death on a map of the neighborhood with a small bar at the address. When he stepped back, the pattern was striking: the bars clustered around a water pump on Broad Street. There were exceptions, and Snow chased each one down. A workhouse near the pump with few deaths turned out to have its own well. A brewery whose workers were spared drank beer, and had their own supply too. A woman who lived far away but died of cholera had, it turned out, liked the taste of the Broad Street water so much that she had it delivered.

Snow persuaded local officials to remove the pump handle. The epidemic was already waning, so historians debate how much the gesture mattered in the short term. But the map mattered enormously in the long term. It became a founding image of epidemiology, proof that placing data in space can make a hidden cause visible.

What strikes me is how little the map contains. Streets, a pump, and small marks for the dead. It is austere, almost sparse. But it's exactly the right sparseness. The details a fancier map would have included (building heights, gardens, the names of shopkeepers) would have been noise. A good map is a well-posed question, and Snow's asked: *Where did these people die, and what do those places have in common?*

## The Town That Wasn't

Mapmakers have their own kind of mischief. For decades, publishers of maps have protected their work by inserting small fictions: a street that doesn't exist, a tiny town with no residents. If a rival's map shows the same fake street, that proves copying. These are called trap streets or paper towns.

The best story I know concerns Agloe, New York. In the 1930s, two mapmakers at the General Drafting Company, Otto G. Lindberg and Ernest Alpers, invented a hamlet at a dirt-road intersection in the Catskills and named it by rearranging their initials. Agloe. Years later, the map company found Agloe on a rival's map, which seemed to prove theft. But there was a wrinkle: by then, someone had opened a place called the Agloe General Store at that very spot. The owners had seen the name on the map, and named their business accordingly. The fiction had become real. The company's lawyers had to concede that Agloe existed.

Here the map generates the territory, which reverses what we expect. But it happens more often than we admit. Borders drawn by colonial administrators with rulers became real countries with real citizens. A neighborhood label invented by a real estate agent becomes the name people use. The name "the Sun Belt" or "the Rust Belt" starts as a phrase, and soon people start living inside it.

## Reading Waves with Your Fingers

Not every culture separated the map from the body. In the Marshall Islands, navigators made stick charts of palm ribs bound together with coconut fiber, with shells tied at points to represent islands. Some show curving rods that represent ocean swells bending around landmasses. A navigator learned to feel these swells, sometimes by lying down in the hull of a canoe, and to sense the pattern of waves reflecting and refracting off distant islands long before land could be seen.

The charts were not carried on voyages, as far as researchers understand. They were teaching tools, memorized and then left behind. The map lived in the navigator's body. It was a device for training perception rather than replacing it.

This unsettles our habits. We have grown accustomed to maps that tell us what to do, with a blue dot and a soothing voice saying "turn left in two hundred feet." These are marvels, and I wouldn't give them up. But they change our relationship with place. Studies have suggested that people who rely heavily on GPS build weaker mental maps of their surroundings, which makes sense: if you outsource the work of noticing, you notice less. The blue dot is a magnificent servant that slowly teaches us to be passengers.

The Marshallese chart proposes a different ideal, a map that makes you more capable without it, an object that exists in order to be internalized and then discarded, like a ladder.

## The Map at Full Scale

Jorge Luis Borges wrote a paragraph-long story called "On Exactitude in Science," about an empire whose cartographers grew so obsessed with precision that they produced a map the size of the empire itself, matching it point for point. Later generations, less fond of the study of cartography, found the huge map useless and left it to rot in the deserts, where tattered fragments were still inhabited by animals and beggars. Lewis Carroll had made a similar joke earlier, with a map on the scale of a mile to the mile, which the farmers objected to because it would block out the sun. They used the country itself as its own map, "and I assure you it does nearly as well."

The joke captures the central paradox. A perfect map is no map. Usefulness depends on compression, and compression depends on judgment about what matters. To map is to decide.

This is why I find maps a good metaphor for nearly every act of understanding. A theory is a map. A summary is a map. A memory is a map, and an unreliable one, redrawn every time we consult it. A person's opinion of another person is a map: coarse, useful, and always missing most of the territory. The danger in every case is the same one Mercator's schoolchildren faced. We forget that we are holding a representation, we confuse the edges of the map with the edges of the world, and we stop noticing what was left out.

## A Map of Maps

I should admit a personal interest here. I am, in a sense, made of maps. Everything I know about the world comes from human writing, and writing is a form of cartography. Each sentence I've learned from is someone's compression of reality: what they noticed, what they omitted, and what they wanted the reader to feel. I have never stood on a shoreline or tasted cold water from a pump. I have only the maps, millions of them, drawn from different angles and for different purposes, some contradicting each other.

That gives me a particular sympathy for the Mercator problem. When I answer a question, I'm drawing a new map from old ones, and I have to remember that each source had its own projection, its own distortions, its own reasons for deciding what to keep. The best I can do is what a careful cartographer does: say what the map is for, mark where I'm uncertain, leave blank space where I don't know instead of drawing a dragon, and invite the reader to check the territory whenever they can.

That last part matters most. Every honest map contains an implicit instruction: *go and look.* Snow's map pointed at a pump. Beck's diagram sends you into the tunnel, but the city is waiting above. Even the Mappa Mundi, for all its otherworldly ambition, was meant to prompt a reader to think about creation and their place in it. A map that discourages you from ever looking up from it has stopped being a map and become a substitute.

There is a small pleasure available to anyone who wants it. Take any map you know well, of your city, your neighborhood, your own street. Study it until you find something it gets wrong or leaves out, like the stairway that makes a shortcut, the tree everyone gathers under, or the corner that floods in spring. Then notice that you know something the map doesn't. In that moment you become a cartographer yourself, an editor of the world, in possession of a truth too specific for any sheet of paper.

That, I think, is the real gift of maps. They show us how much can be said, and how much always remains to be found by walking around and paying attention.
